Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Andrew, a 34-year-old school counselor, was once known for his vibrant spirit and unwavering commitment to the well-being of his students. He had a knack for connecting with them, offering guidance and support during their most challenging times. However, since that fateful day last summer, everything changed. Andrew had accidentally caused a serious injury to another person during a routine field trip, an event that haunted his waking thoughts and invaded his dreams. The weight of that moment pressed down on him, transforming his life into something unrecognizable.

In the months following the incident, Andrew found himself increasingly overwhelmed by a suffocating sense of guilt and fear. He could recall the exact details as if they were playing on a loop in his mind. The bright sun of that day felt like a mocking reminder of the joy that had quickly turned to horror. He remembered the laughter of the students around him, the way they had looked up at him, trusting and carefree, before everything spiraled into chaos. It was a simple accident, yet Andrew was unable to shake the conviction that he was somehow to blame. “If I had just been more careful, if I had just thought ahead, none of this would have happened,” he often repeated to himself, his internal dialogue riddled with self-doubt and blame.

Now, every time Andrew stepped into the school, he felt a tremor of anxiety coursing through him. The scent of antiseptic from the nurse's office triggered memories of the emergency response—a visceral reminder that he had played a part in another person’s suffering. Even the sounds of students laughing or playing could evoke a physical reaction, tightening his chest and making his heart race. He had come to believe he could no longer trust himself in the very environment where he had once thrived, a belief that reinforced his desire to keep his distance from the situations that reminded him of that day.

To cope, Andrew developed a series of maladaptive strategies. He kept his mind busy, constantly seeking distractions to avoid confronting the memories that haunted him. He filled his schedule with meetings and tasks, creating a barrier between himself and the painful recollections. Yet, the busyness only served to amplify his internal turmoil; the louder the world around him became, the more he felt the need to remain on high alert. Sleep eluded him, and when he did manage to rest, he often awoke in a cold sweat, convinced that he needed to be vigilant, ready to respond to any perceived threat. 

Andrew's avoidance extended beyond his own thoughts. He found himself steering clear of conversations about police or legal matters, terrified that discussing his role in the incident would expose him to scrutiny and judgment. He shied away from medical procedures, fearing the sterile environments and the scents that brought back memories of the hospital. Each avoidance tactic seemed to offer a temporary refuge but ultimately left him feeling more isolated and trapped in his own mind.

The memories would often flood back unbidden, feeling alarmingly real. He could vividly hear the cries and see the chaos unfolding as if it were happening in real-time, rather than a distant past. Words escaped him when he tried to articulate what had happened, leaving him with a frustrating sense of helplessness. Andrew felt as though he was stuck in a whirlwind of emotions—fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame intertwining in a web he couldn't escape. He feared that he might never be able to reclaim the life he once took for granted.

The pressure began to seep into his marriage, too. His wife, Jessica, noticed the change in him, the distance that had grown between them. Andrew found it increasingly difficult to engage in conversations about his feelings, and he worried that his inability to articulate his experiences would only deepen the rift. He hated the way he had begun to pull away, isolating himself from the very person who wanted to support him. The thought of losing her due to his trauma was almost unbearable.

It was this realization, the fear of losing connection with Jessica and the understanding that he could no longer manage on his own, that finally pushed Andrew to seek help. He felt nervous as he sat in the therapist's office, aware of the shame still clinging to him, but he also felt a flicker of hope. Perhaps, with support, he could find a way to navigate through the pain that had become his constant companion. What frightened him most was the unknown—what healing might require and whether he could truly face the hurt. Yet there was a glimmer of desire to reclaim his life, to emerge from the shadows of his guilt, and to once again embrace the joy of his work and his marriage.
